Could you please have a look at paragraph 3 of this dispatch which says: "The MUP staff in Pristina will propose employees who have been engaged on special security tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija for decorations, early promotions, or awards." My question for you is the following: Could you propose any employees who were engaged in the special security tasks for decorations, early promotions, or awards? That is to say, your members of the Special Police unit which you sent to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already discussed this at length, and we noted that by sending Special Police units to carry out special security tasks in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, all the authority that the chief of secretariat had over them were temporarily frozen, and in connection with paragraph 3 of this dispatch which was sent to all chiefs of secretariats, I was not informed about what was being done down there, how, in what manner, how did the men conduct during the anti-terrorist operations, how did they carry out their regular duties and tasks. Only the staff and the commanding officers who directly commanded these units in Kosovo and Metohija could know that. Therefore, I could not in any event propose these employees, that is to say, these policemen who were members of special units sent there for any decorations or awards.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. This is the last document I will show you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see D254.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Which is your tab 47. Mr. Pantelic, this is dispatch number 1015 dated the 4th of May, 1999. It says, SUP all the chief signed by assistant minister chief of sector, Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic. Could you please look at this dispatch more closely, especially the first paragraph. If you could please comment on this and say if these were duties and tasks which you focused on during the NATO bombing campaign. Later on we shall also focus on the measures, which are mentioned, in the next part of this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this dispatch, at least with this I have some experience because Valjevo was bombed 21 times during the NATO war operations, the relevant measures and activities needed to be taken and carried out in order to address the situation in the best possible manner. In that sense, this dispatch was formulated. The idea was to save human lives and property. It is noted that the members of the ministry have displayed high levels of professionalism, expertise, and extreme dedication in their interventions, however, members of this ministry have also been injured during the interventions. What is requested by this dispatch confirms once again what we had been doing in continuity even before all that, that the places where NATO would attack needed to be identified, then these places needed to be secured by the necessary number of policemen, the traffic needed to be redirected so that the citizens would be protected. Also, the timely arrival of firefighters and ambulances needed to be assured. Then it said that first aid needed to be provided to the employees who were injured, that the fires needed to be extinguished, that we should take into account human lives and try to save them. So fires should be extinguished only when it's save and secure and when it is necessary, when there is a possibility to save a part of a facility that was hit. And also to use the equipment in a rational and cautious manner. So that was the gist of this dispatch which was sent by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you had great experience and that Valjevo and the territory of your secretariat was unfortunately bombed 21 times. What was the procedure for the secretariat after each of the bombings? What did do you, who did you report to, and in what way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance to the rules of the organisation of the Ministry of the Interior I directly reported for my work to the chief of the public security sector. That means that I had in any case to report to him about the situation which were the result of the attacks of NATO air force. I had to report to him which facilities were hit, what was the damage, were there any casualties, and what were the measures that needed to be taken in order to address the situation. In addition to the fact that I reported to him personally, the duty service of my secretariat sent reports along its own line to the operations centre of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, my direct question is whether after each NATO attack you personally reported to Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the nature of things, I was obliged to report to him, and I did that in every situation when that was possible. If I did not manage to get in touch with him on one specific day, if he was away at a certain time and we also had problems with telephone lines, I would manage to reach him in a day or two, then we got in touch with each other, we talked. I also went to Belgrade to his war-time location while he was stationed in Lola Ivo Ribar Street, and I reported to him about the problems that we are talking about now. So I had frequent contacts with him through special telephone lines up until the moment when the building of the secretariat of the MUP in Valjevo was destroyed by NATO aircraft projectiles, and later I used the regular phone lines because the -- the telephone switchboards for special lines had been destroyed. We tended to avoid cell phones because none of the relay systems or base stations which conveyed the impulses of cell phones were not bombed, and we knew that the aggressor was listening to all of our conversations. That was why we avoided mobile telephone lines, and we talked either on secure telephone lines or more rarely through regular telephone lines, or we had personal contacts. In addition to that, the courier service operated between Valjevo and Belgrade twice a week so that we also conveyed information by that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in your personal contacts with Mr. Djordjevic. First of all, when you contacted him through these special telephone lines, where did you call him, and how did you get in touch with him by using these special telephone lines? That is to say, where was the special telephone which you called located?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called special, that is to say the special telephone, it is a secure line, was in the office of the chief of the sector. I think that in addition to that, there was another one which the head of his office had. However, I could rarely reach the head of office. Most often the chief of the sector would answer the phone when I used this telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And physically where was the office of the chief of sector, so the office in which that telephone that you called was placed in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the war operations I would reach him within the building of the Ministry of the Interior, the building that was later on destroyed. And later I spoke to him while he was in Lola Ivo Ribar Street in Belgrade. This is where I also visited him on several occasions. These were the premises of a bank, I believe the commercial bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. And to finish with, I would like to ask you, do you know Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Djordjevic ever since 1971 or 1972. At the time he was still chief for control of the legality of operations of the Ministry of the Interior. So I have known him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship like with Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always had very correct professional relationship with Mr. Djordjevic, and it was not all only about work. When he was still chief of police at the Ministry of the Interior, I would often visit him. We talked about our duties, but we also discussed other tasks, and we would also spend some time simply about talking -- simply talking about one thing or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you try to remember how many times you saw him during the year 1999, and where precisely.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1999, as I said, we were constantly in touch by phone, and we saw one another in his war-time office. Whether it was three or four times, I can't really recall, but I do know that I went there certainly on several occasions, and in addition to the problems related to NATO aggression, I also had some human resources problem at the level of my secretariat, and these problems had to be urgently resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please make it more precise when you say "war-time office." What was the address of that office? So the town, the street.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact address, but I believe it was Lola Ivo Ribar Street, this is next to Tasmajdanski Park.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What is the city that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, did you ever during the course of 1998 or 1999 see or hear that there was any plan within the Ministry of the Interior, the goal of which was to expel the Albanian population from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absurd to talk about any such plan. Why would we wait for 55 years after the end of the Second World War, and why would we wait for the NATO aggression to carry out any such plan? It simply makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, did you ever during the course of 1998 or 1999 hear or see of any plan within the Ministry of the Interior the goal of which would be to expel the Albanian population from Kosovo in order to modify the ethnic balance within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question is very much related to your previous one, and it is an absurd topic to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, but that is the reason why we are here. It is not all that absurd, so I would kindly ask you to give me a precise answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My precise answer is that I never heard of any such plan, and I wouldn't even know what that plan would be all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with this I have completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Mr. Stamp, is it convenient now, or should we take the break a few minutes early?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a matter for the Court. We could take the break, I have no real issues with when we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think for everybody it would be a good idea to mark this change with the break now, and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, are you currently employed, or you are fully retired?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not employed. I have been retired since the 30th of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So after the 30th of December, 2001, did you participate at all in any type of employment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not been engaged in any work for remuneration. I'm just president of the hunting society of Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you since your retirement been active in any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not engaged in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become the head of SUP in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became chief of SUP in Valjevo in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. In respect to the previous question you said you are not engaged in politics. What I asked you is whether or not since your retirement you ever were engaged in any type of political activity, that is, any time after your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I retired, all my political activities ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to your retirement, what type of political activity were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that precisely. I was a member for a while, maybe for four or five years, and then I stopped being a member immediately prior to the beginning of the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is, you stopped being a member about the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it came about that you stopped being a member?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several reasons, and I believe these reasons were of a personal nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it was at your motion, at your -- well, by your action that your relationship with the socialist party was terminated?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was at my own will only, and part of the reason was that I was dissatisfied with the work of certain structures within the political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you after that for any period, however short of time, get active or engage in any other type of political work with any other political organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I was never a member of any political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But notwithstanding your not being a member, did you at any time engage in any type of political activity with or on behalf of any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never been engaged in any such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you attended -- no, well, you didn't say. You said that there were meetings approximately once every three months, approximately five for the year with the minister, the assistant ministers, and the chief of SUPs, and the head of their lines within the ministry, within the public service department. Did you attend all of these meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but I believe I did attend them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were any of these meetings kept in 1999, or convened in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I can't say that for sure. I believe the last meeting was the one in which we discussed the results of our work in 1998, so I believe there were no meetings at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were collegiums or collegiums of the minister of interior that were held in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about some collegiums in a previous period, but I didn't know who attended them or what was the role, the function of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you never attended any meeting of the collegium of the minister or the collegium of the chief of public security department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended any meeting of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you attend any meetings at all which involved the minister Stojiljkovic where he delineated the authority of his assistant ministers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only attended one meeting at which the minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic was present. And this was a meeting at which we discussed the construction of a new building of the secretariat of the interior in Valjevo because NATO aviation destroyed the secretariat building in May. At that meeting possibly there were three or four assistants or chiefs of administrations, but I can't say that there was any conflict expressed there, and there was also no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about conflicts, but I think you have answered the question. Your conclusions, some of which you stated here, about the various roles of assistant ministers and also of the chief of the crime police department, Mr. Ilic, is based, I take it, on what you heard from various people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my conclusions are based both on what I heard from others and also on the content and the method in which dispatches were sent and received by my Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you see any dispatch that indicated to you that Mr. Ilic was independent of the chief of public security?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have probably received such a dispatch. I never saw it. Whether any such dispatch was sent or not, I don't know, but as I said previously from my conversations with Dragan Ilic, I could conclude that he answered directly to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also in the course of your evidence, you were commenting on some reports that you received from the headquarters in Belgrade. I think D415 is one of them. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we just have a quick look at that just to make sure we are talking about the same document. D415 is not one of them. D411, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are dispatches, all of those dispatches that are shown, the daily reports, these are dispatches that were sent from headquarters in Belgrade for the information of the various persons to whom they were addressed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not -- well, obviously on the face of it this is not the reports that were sent to Belgrade from the various SUPs and other departments of the -- other sectors of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a short while ago that this was a daily review of current events and occurrences in the public security area for one single day, so it is based on information received from all the secretariats. That information went to Belgrade, the received information was processed by the analysis administration, and then on the basis of cumulative information received from all the secretariats, the ministry would send out such a daily review.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the chief of the public security department was your direct superior. Wasn't he also the direct superior of all of the chiefs of SUPs in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our rules of organisation within the Ministry of the Interior, he was superior to all the chiefs of secretariats in the territory of Serbia except for the Autonomous Province of Kosovo because the minister adopted a decision to set up the staff there, thus establishing different structures, organisational structures there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to that decision, that is the decision to set up the staff. But can you just tell us whether or not there is any rule or law that exempted the SUPs in Kosovo or any SUP chief? May I just repeat the question. I withdraw it. Can you tell us whether there was any law, rule, or regulation that exempted the chief of the secretariats, any chief of secretariat in Kosovo from the direct authority of the chief of public security?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such legal provision in the law on the Internal Affairs. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there any rule, law, or regulation, any at all, that exempted any SUP chief from their responsibilities as subordinates of the chief of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a legal provision did not exist. However, if you allow me to say, in order on the basis of which the minister set up the staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina was based on the authorities given to him by the law on the Internal Affairs and the law on state administration. The minister was authorised by those pieces of legislation to adopt regulations, rules, instructions, and decisions. So by adopting a decision on the setup of the staff, the minister simply brought to life the authority that he was given by the existing legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, we'll get to that document. But while we are on it, it is your position then that the reason why you say that SUP chiefs in Kosovo were not the subordinates of Mr. Djordjevic is because of the decision he adopted setting up the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a decision made by the minister in which it is listed that all organisational units in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo are under the command of the staff in Pristina. That is in the documents which you have at your disposal and which I have seen here during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you reported directly to Mr. Djordjevic, both in person and by telephone and by sending other reports. Yes, you said it. Weren't all the SUPs in Serbia obliged to report to Mr. Djordjevic, the chief of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our rules on organisations are such that we are directly subordinated to the chief of the public security sector. Therefore, we were obliged to report to him and resolve the current security problems together with him in an appropriate manner. I'm not saying that we did not contact the lines of work within the ministry, that is to say the assistant ministers. We did contact them as well, but in practice, they were not our superior organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, weren't the other SUP chiefs obliged to report to Mr. Djordjevic just as you were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was valid for me was also valid for other chiefs of secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Including those in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those in Kosovo, the chiefs of secretariats in Kosovo were placed under the command of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if they reported to Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't talk about that because I was not informed about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Sreten Lukic, who was the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly knew him. I had known him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long? How long before 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly more than ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he reported to Mr. Djordjevic in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not a member of the forces stationed in the territory of the province, and I cannot be positive about whether he sent reports or did not send them, but according to this decision to set up the staff, the commander of the staff was directly responsible to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, since you keep raising it, maybe we could bring it up. What number? P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this decision that you hinge so much on? I see it's there. Is it there now? No, it's not. Is it addressed -- well, before you get to my last question, may I just ask you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps you could go to the next page, the last page of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it seems based on the last part there before the signature of the minister that you were not one of the persons to whom it was sent. When was the first time you saw this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this decision until I came here and started preparations for this trial. I never saw the decision previously nor was I aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know about the real arrangements for monitoring, deploying forces in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just say that I did not see this decision of the minister, but I did have frequent contacts, and it was logical that I would know who would I be sending my men to, so I had telephone contacts and direct contacts in 1999, and in 1998 I went to the staff of the ministry and I knew who my three companies would be subordinated to and who they would report to. This is why I mentioned all this. And as for the decision to establish the staff, I saw it for the first time when I came here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Djordjevic's role was in Kosovo in 1998 after this decision was issued, that is 16th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you said he was down there during anti-terrorist operation that they had in the summer, which ended in the autumn, in October 1998 he was down there quite a lot on the instructions of the minister. Would you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I contacted him regularly. I know that he was away for a while, but what duties he had to perform, I really did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even though this question was responded to, what is mentioned here as the assertion of the witness is not something that the witness mentioned, so I would ask Mr. Stamp to give a reference for this, that he knew that he was down there during anti-terrorist operations, that they had there in the summer which ended in the autumn of 1998. I don't remember that the witness ever mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the gravamen of the witness testimony. He said that many times. I could -- I thought it was well known, but I could provide the references later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps at a convenient time you could provide them to Mr. Popovic and the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document. This is P1507.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could look at the last three questions -- I will just tell you this. This is answers given to -- answers given by Mr. Sreten Lukic the question that you asked of him, and I'd like you to read the last three questions and answers of that page, and could we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a document is being used which Mr. Lukic provided as a suspect, and these are his answers to questions asked by the investigator. The Trial Chamber already took its stand concerning this. I have nothing against Mr. Stamp presenting certain parts of these answers to the witness, whether he knows that Mr. Lukic said that, but I think this might not be the appropriate manner to use this document as the Trial Chamber has already expressed its position about this document. Thank you, that will be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question I propose to ask is directly in line with the instructions by the Trial Chamber when this document was last used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you look at the first question now on the next page and the answer thereto. Now, Mr. Pantelic, the question is this, and I ask you the question because you have given us a lot of conclusion based on hearsay and what other people have said to you. Now, having read this from Mr. Lukic, can you tell us what are your conclusions in respect to the command relationship between Mr. Lukic and Mr. Djordjevic in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about their relations in Kosovo because I do not know what these relations were. What I said during my testimony was based on appropriate documents which I interpreted. Whatever I said was based on certain documents. There are statements here of persons who were accused and some of them were sentenced, but I wouldn't go into that. And I really was not informed about their relations there in the territory of Kosovo. I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many times Mr. Djordjevic went to Kosovo for purposes of work in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that because I'm not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many times he went down there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that either. I cannot be positive about that. I remember that I managed to reach him in his office quite often, but how many times he went there during the war, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether he went there at all during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I had so many problems to deal with that I was really not in the situation to follow the situation within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, you were focused on your problems in Valjevo? Is that right, what I just said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mostly focused on these problems because, as I recently noted, the NATO air force targeted targets in Valjevo on 21 occasions. But regardless of that, we had to perform our regular duties from the remit of work of the ministry, and by nature of things, we were obliged to report to the ministry about duties discharged, and in that sense, I did have several telephone conversations, and I did meet the chief of the sector, but I couldn't tell you when exactly that was. I cannot remember the exact date nor even the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you consider Mr. Djordjevic to be a friend?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said during my testimony that our relations were proper, professional relations. We did not socialise privately, but as far as work is concerned, we could find common ground in connection with many problems, and on the basis of that, I can say that we did have -- that we were close to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you maintain contact with him after the war in 2000, the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any special contacts. He was not the chief of sector anymore, and I had to regulate security problems about the entry into the zones in Kosovo and the southern Serbia in an action which involved international forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about the year 2000. I believe Mr. Djordjevic was -- well, I don't know if he was relieved of his duties, but he ceased being the chief of the public security department in 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001 as I tried to say a while ago, I saw him in April or May in Presevo or in Bujanovac, and that was the last time when I saw him in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We need to clarify that. The evidence before the Court is that by May 2001 after it became public that some corpses were found at a place called Batajnica, Mr. Djordjevic could not be found. Do you remember that that is what transpired in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened when this problem around Batajnica arose. I cannot remember the date, but as I say, I saw Mr. Djordjevic down there when the international forces entered the southern part of Serbia, that was the last time when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't that have been in May 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not in 2000. That was in, just a second, in April or May, but not the year 2000, but rather 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We have some evidence before the Court that there was a body set up in Kosovo known as a Joint Command. Have you ever heard of this body?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard that it was extended, and that the staff of the ministry in Pristina was extended by members of state security who were added to it. This is what I know about the problem. And two days ago I saw here in these proceedings a document which was an order to establish the staff from which I could see who were the members of the staff. Until I saw the document, I had not known who were the members of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was talking about another body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P886.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of Mr. Djordjevic being a member of or a participant of any command body, and when I say "command body," a body for commanding operations, anti-terrorist operations of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure whether the OTP notified us about this document in their notice, that they would be using it, and therefore, we cannot find it in our system. So I apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, if we have it, but we cannot find it on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the last item on the list. It's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at page 24 of this document. I'm sorry, I think we have the wrong page. I think we want page 41 both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without us having to click back and forth, this is a meeting of the 12th of August, 1998, some two months after that decision by the minister. You see a record here of General Djordjevic in a meeting with General Stevanovic and General Pavkovic being recorded as saying that the 3rd and 4th Detachments should be engaged, as well as the army. Do you see Mr. Djordjevic speaking at this meeting? Well, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text in English language and some notes from a notebook. Someone's notes, but I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read in the middle of the page what General Djordjevic is recorded as having said in your language?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot see anything here in my own language except for these handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read those notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwriting is very bad. If somebody could help me because I'm really not able to decipher it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will. General Djordjevic said or recorded to have said: "Engage the 3rd and 4th Detachments around Loda and have them work on Friday. Do Voksa and Slup and engage the army." I show you this as an example. Do you know of General Djordjevic participating in meetings of a body called the Joint Command that was responsible for anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see that, and I was really never informed about this anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you were standing a moment ago. Is there some matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I just thought that, first of all, we were supposed to establish whether the witness knew anything about this, whether he ever saw this document, and only then proceed with the questions. This was my only suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we look at P357. That's the rules of internal organisation of the MUP. And we could go straight to Article 54. I think it's page 43 in the English. Article 54 is page 42 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's quite basic. According to the governing rules, it says that the department shall be controlled by the chief of the department. Can you read Article 54?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is hardly legible, but I'm trying to read it. Yes, I think I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Djordjevic for quite a long time, and you had to associate with him on quite a few occasions in your professional capacity. Did Mr. Djordjevic demonstrate to you in your years of knowing him that he knew what his legal powers and authority were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed any legal authorities. There was a lawyer at the level of the Ministry of the Interior and at the level of secretariats. We all had these rules of organisation, but we never discussed any such matter. There was simply no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. Djordjevic appear to you to be the type of leader or commander who would be unaware that the law empowered him to control the department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an exceptionally positive opinion about Mr. Djordjevic. Now, how much was he aware of the provisions of these rules, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You think that it is possible that Mr. Djordjevic might not have been aware that the law empowered him to control operations of the public security department? That that was his responsibility by law?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me whether he was aware, I am sure he was. Now, the question is to what -- or how much could he do if he had a superior who established different organisational relationships at a level of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us already that you were not present when Mr. Stojiljkovic met with Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present at any meeting of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you have a very positive assessment of Mr. Djordjevic. In your assessment was he a strong leader, or would you say that he was a weak leader, easily influenced and would yield to pressure?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an answer, I would offer something in the middle range. So he was as strong as others permitted him to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that's an almost meaningless answer, Mr. Pantelic. Let me ask you more direct question then. Do you think he would be strong enough as a man with this legal authority that you see here to withstand pressures and influences from anybody that he commit crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not believe that he would participate in any activity related to a crime of any kind. This is my personal view, my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I'm concerned that you are straying beyond the bounds of reasonable and proper cross-examination. You based your questions on speculation. The witness says that he does not have the knowledge that you postulate your questions on. I've given you a fairly free hand to date, but I really think you are pushing out too far now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- well, very well, Your Honours, I will -- I will limit myself to the areas that he says that he is aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic said that -- well, let me withdraw the question. Do you in your assessment of your commander assess him as someone who could be pressured to conceal the crime of murder?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question, and I really could not answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you said that you were in Mr. Stojiljkovic's office -- sorry, Mr. Ilic's office, and Mr. Stojiljkovic called and gave instructions. Do you know what the instructions were about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has been over ten years ago. I can't possibly remember what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Ilic who told you that it was the minister who was calling?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the minister called him and that he called him twice during one hour. Possibly he said something more, but I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have some evidence before the Court that there were efforts made to retrieve some bodies that were found in the Danube. And it was Mr. Ilic who made the arrangements for the persons who were involved in retrieving and concealing these bodies to be paid for their services. Do you know who instructed Mr. Ilic to attend to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that event in the newspapers, as did all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia [as interpreted]. I was never in a situation in which anybody conveyed any information to me concerning this particular event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect the answer page 72, line 4 referred to the Republic of Serbia, not Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you mean that you don't know how Mr. Ilic got involved in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, let's move on to something you probably know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at P58. That is the decision to set up the PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it time enough to refer to a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is probably a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and resume again tomorrow afternoon at 2.15

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
